items.title: About the Wallaroos
items.text:
The Wallaroos played their first Test on 2 September 1994, against New Zealand in Sydney. Four years later they made their first Rugby World Cup appearance.

Their best World Cup finish is third place, in 2010. Since 2018 Super W has given the country’s best players a national club competition and a clearer path into the Wallaroos.

data.headline: Super W and the road to the Wallaroos
data.standfirst: Since 2018, Super W has given Australia’s best women players a national club competition.

image.alt: A women’s match: a ball carrier in white tackled by players in navy and red

body.text: Super W began in 2018. It brings together teams from around the country and gives the best women players regular, high-level games outside the international season.
Before Super W, the step from club rugby to the Wallaroos was a big one. A national competition lets selectors see players against strong opposition week after week.
With the Women’s Rugby World Cup coming to Australia in 2029, the pathway from club and school rugby through Super W to the Wallaroos has never mattered more.

data.headline: The Wallaroos: the story so far
data.standfirst: The Wallaroos played their first Test on 2 September 1994, against New Zealand in Sydney. Four years later they made their first Rugby World Cup appearance.

image.alt: Players in maroon jerseys arm in arm in a team huddle

body.text: Their best World Cup finish is third place, in 2010. Since 2018 Super W has given the country’s best players a national club competition and a clearer path into the Wallaroos.
In 2029 Australia hosts the Women’s Rugby World Cup for the first time.
Players reach the Wallaroos through club rugby, state teams and the national pathway. Every player who pulls on the jersey gets a cap number, counting every international since the first.

data.headline: A first-timer’s guide to a Test match
data.standfirst: Going to your first international? Here is how to make the most of the day.

image.alt: A floodlit stadium packed with spectators

body.text: A Test match is the biggest day on the rugby calendar. Crowds are bigger than at club or Super Rugby games, so a little planning goes a long way.
Public transport is usually the easiest way to reach the stadium. Gates open about two hours before kick-off, and arriving early means you see the warm-ups and are in your seat for the anthems.
Wear the colours and bring a jacket for night games. Kids are welcome, and many stadiums have family areas.
Expect queues for transport after the final whistle. Staying for a drink or a bite while the crowd clears often makes for an easier trip home.
